title_original: Lost ‘Faust Bible’ Unearthed And Published For F.W. Murnau’s Silent Masterpiece’s 100th Anniversary
excerpt_original: To mark the 100th anniversary of F.W. Murnau’s silent cinema masterpiece Faust (1926), MUBI, in partnership with La Cinémathèque française, has announced the international release of The Faust Bible: The Making of F.W. Murnau’s Masterpiece. The book is set for release on October…

blocks.text: To mark the 100th anniversary of F.W. Murnau’s silent cinema masterpiece Faust (1926), MUBI, in partnership with La Cinémathèque française, has announced the international release of The Faust Bible: The Making of F.W. Murnau’s Masterpiece .

The book is set for release on October 17, 2026, and recreates a recently unearthed artefact of film history: a visual diary of approximately 400 photographs and original illustrations documenting the making of the film almost step-by-step. Originally compiled by crew members Robert Herlth, Carl Hoffmann, and Walter Röhrig, the collection was presented to Murnau inside a prop Bible as a memento upon the completion of filming, right before his move from Germany to Hollywood. Long thought to have been destroyed during the Second World War, the volume survived, was hidden for decades, and was eventually rediscovered and restored by La Cinémathèque française after they acquired it in 2017.

Now published in full for the very first time, the book features stills and sketches that showcase the skill at the heart of Murnau’s production, including innovative practical effects, lavish costuming, set design, and detailed storyboarding. Daniel Kasman, MUBI’s Vice President of Publishing, noted that the discovery offers new insight into the mind of one of cinema’s greatest auteurs, revealing the meticulous artistry behind a groundbreaking visual fantasia.

Based on Goethe’s classic drama and German folklore, Murnau’s 1926 masterpiece is a towering work of Expressionism centering on a celestial wager where the demon Mephisto corrupts an aging alchemist. Desperate to save his plague-stricken village, Faust signs away his soul for renewed youth and power, embarking on a tragic journey of debauchery and star-crossed love with the innocent Gretchen before their ultimate redemption through love in the flames.

The milestone publication arrives amidst a broader celebration of Murnau’s visionary career, which included directing 21 films that cemented his legacy as one of the most inventive figures of the silent era before his tragic death in an automobile accident in 1931 at age 42. While nearly half of his filmography – including his very first feature, The Boy in Blue (1919) – was lost over time, his surviving works showcase his mastery of light, shadow, and mobile camera techniques. Among his most celebrated and enduring achievements is Nosferatu (1922), an unauthorized adaptation of Bram Stoker’s Dracula that introduced Max Schreck as the haunting Count Orlok and became a foundational pillar of horror cinema. He followed this with The Last Laugh (1924), a tragedy starring Emil Jannings that famously omitted intertitles in favor of fluid, pioneering camera movements by cinematographer Karl Freund.

Invited to Hollywood by producer William Fox, Murnau directed the romantic masterpiece Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927), which won three awards at the Academy Awards and remains widely considered one of the greatest films ever made due to its breathtaking tracking shots and emotional depth. His later works include Tartuffe (1925), the satirical framing-device drama City Girl (1930), and Tabu: A Story of the South Seas (1931), a visually stunning romantic tragedy co-directed with Robert J. Flaherty on location in Bora Bora, from which Murnau tragically passed away just one week before its New York premiere.

Faust (1926) will arrive on the MUBI platform to stream globally starting on October 14, with live-scored centenary screenings in Paris on 17 October, Munich on 25 October, and Los Angeles on 1 November . The global publication launches on October 17, from mubieditions.com .
